claim: FGF14 co-immunoprecipitates with NaV1.6 channels in mouse cerebellar lysates.
source: Although FGF14 was previously shown to co-immunoprecipitate with NaV1.6 in a heterologous expression system (Laezza et al., 2009), co-immunoprecipitation between FGF14 and NaV1.6 channels has not been reported from brain.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating co-immunoprecipitation from mouse cerebellum.

claim: FGF14 knockdown does not affect NaV current density in cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: Knockdown of FGF14 did not affect NaV current density compared to the NaV current density recorded in neurons transfected with a control shRNA (Figure 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B comparing current-voltage relationships.

claim: FGF14 knockdown does not affect voltage dependence of NaV channel activation.
source: Voltage dependence of activation was unaffected by FGF14 knockdown (Figure 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Table 1.

claim: FGF14 knockdown shifts the V1/2 of steady-state inactivation by about −10 mV, thereby decreasing channel availability.
source: but the V1/2 of steady-state inactivation was shifted about −10 mV, thereby decreasing channel availability (Figure 2B and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: Co-expression of shRNA-resistant FGF14bWT restores the V1/2 of steady-state inactivation to control voltage after FGF14 knockdown.
source: When we co-expressed a FGF14b cDNA with synonymous substitutions rendering it resistant to the FGF14 shRNA (FGF14bWT), the V1/2 of steady-state inactivation was restored to the control voltage; activation was unaffected (Figure 2A–B and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B and Table 1.

claim: FGF14 knockdown accelerates NaV channel inactivation kinetics.
source: In addition to the decreased channel availability, we observed that FGF14 knockdown accelerated inactivation kinetics (Figure 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: FGF14 knockdown reduces the late NaV current.
source: FGF14 knockdown also reduced the late NaV current (Figure 2E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E-F.

claim: FGF14 knockdown biases endogenous NaV channels towards entering the inactivated state.
source: Thus, by several different kinetic measures, FGF14 knockdown in cerebellar Purkinje neurons biased the endogenous NaV channels towards entering the inactivated state.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental observations including decreased channel availability, accelerated inactivation kinetics, and reduced late current.

claim: FGF14 knockdown markedly diminishes the amplitude of resurgent NaV current.
source: Indeed, the amplitude of the resurgent NaV current (Figure 2G–J) was markedly diminished using a well-established protocol to elicit NaV resurgent current (Raman and Bean, 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-J and cites an established protocol.

claim: Co-expression of FGF14bWT provides complete rescue of resurgent NaV current after FGF14 knockdown.
source: As with the other kinetic properties of NaV currents (above), co-expression of FGF14bWT in the presence of the shRNA provided a complete rescue (Figure 2G–J).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G-J.

claim: FGF14 knockdown does not significantly affect the time to peak of resurgent NaV current.
source: While FGF14 knockdown reduced the amplitude of resurgent NaV current, it did not significantly affect the time to peak (Figure 2K).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2K.

claim: FGF14b is the predominant FGF14 splice variant expressed in brain.
source: FGF14b is the predominant FGF14 splice variant expressed in brain (Wang et al., 2000, 2011) and the FGF14 splice variant found in the cytoplasm; FGF14a is localized to the nucleus (Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: FGF14a is localized to the nucleus.
source: FGF14b is the predominant FGF14 splice variant expressed in brain (Wang et al., 2000, 2011) and the FGF14 splice variant found in the cytoplasm; FGF14a is localized to the nucleus (Wang et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Deletion of the FGF14 N-terminus does not affect interaction with the NaV CTD.
source: Because the interaction site for the NaV CTD on FHFs lies within the conserved core domain (Wang et al., 2012), deletion of the N-terminus does not affect interaction with the NaV CTD.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge from a cited study about the interaction site location.

claim: FGF14ΔNT exerts a dominant negative effect by competing with endogenous FGF14 for interaction with the NaV CTD.
source: Thus, the FGF14ΔNT exerts a dominant negative effect by competing with endogenous FGF14 for interaction with the NaV CTD (Figure 3A).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the knowledge that deletion of N-terminus does not affect CTD binding and experimental design shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Expression of FGF14ΔNT does not affect NaV current density.
source: Current density (Figure 3B) and the V1/2 of activation (Figure 3C and Table 1) were unaffected.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Expression of FGF14ΔNT does not affect the V1/2 of activation.
source: Current density (Figure 3B) and the V1/2 of activation (Figure 3C and Table 1) were unaffected.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Table 1.

claim: Expression of FGF14ΔNT shifts the V1/2 of steady-state inactivation about −10 mV.
source: However, expression of FGF14ΔNT shifted the V1/2 of steady-state inactivation about −10 mV (Figure 3C)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Expression of FGF14ΔNT accelerates kinetics of inactivation.
source: However, expression of FGF14ΔNT shifted the V1/2 of steady-state inactivation about −10 mV (Figure 3C), accelerated kinetics of inactivation (Figure 3D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Expression of FGF14ΔNT reduces the late NaV current.
source: However, expression of FGF14ΔNT shifted the V1/2 of steady-state inactivation about −10 mV (Figure 3C), accelerated kinetics of inactivation (Figure 3D), reduced the late NaV current (Figure 3E)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Expression of FGF14ΔNT diminishes resurgent current.
source: However, expression of FGF14ΔNT shifted the V1/2 of steady-state inactivation about −10 mV (Figure 3C), accelerated kinetics of inactivation (Figure 3D), reduced the late NaV current (Figure 3E), and diminished resurgent current (Figure 3F) to a degree similar to or even greater than shRNA knockdown.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: FGF14ΔNT diminishes resurgent NaV current more effectively than shRNA knockdown of FGF14.
source: FGF14ΔNT diminished resurgent NaV current even more effectively than shRNA knockdown of FGF14.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of experimental data from Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Overexpression of FGF14bWT has no effect on NaV channel parameters in cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: Overexpression of FGF14bWT here was without effect (Figure 3 and Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: Endogenous FGF14b is saturating in cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: Not only did this serve as a control for FGF14ΔNT, but these data suggest that endogenous FGF14b is saturating.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that overexpression of FGF14bWT has no effect.

claim: FGF14b's main regulatory component for Purkinje neuron NaV currents lies within the FGF14b N-terminus.
source: These data also suggest that FGF14b's main regulatory component for Purkinje neuron NaV currents lies within the FGF14b N-terminus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the dominant negative effects of FGF14ΔNT.

claim: Arg57 in FGF13 (equivalent to Arg117 in FGF14b) inserts into a deep pocket on the NaV1.5 CTD binding surface.
source: We focused on a highly conserved Arg in the FHF core domain (Arg57 in FGF13U, equivalent to Arg117 in FGF14b), which inserts into a deep pocket on the NaV1.5 CTD binding surface (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is based on structural data from a cited study and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The FGF14bR/A mutant is unable to co-immunoprecipitate NaV1.6.
source: Although immunoprecipitation of FGF14bWT from lysates of HEK293 cells transfected with FGF14bWT and NaV1.6 showed co-immunoprecipitation of NaV1.6, the mutant FGF14bR/A was unable to co-immunoprecipitate NaV1.6 (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Mutation of R117A in FGF14b prevents interaction with NaV1.6.
source: Thus, mutation of R117A in FGF14b prevents interaction with NaV1.6.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Expression of FGF14bR/A after shRNA knockdown of endogenous FGF14 has no effect on NaV current density.
source: Expression of FGF14bR/A after shRNA knockdown of endogenous FGF14 had no effect on NaV current density (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: FGF14bR/A does not rescue NaV late current after FGF14 shRNA knockdown.
source: In contrast to the rescue afforded by FGF14bWT, FGF14bR/A did not rescue the key parameters that lead to increased inactivation observed after FGF14 shRNA. NaV late current and the time constant of inactivation were not different from shRNA (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: FGF14bR/A does not rescue the time constant of inactivation after FGF14 shRNA knockdown.
source: In contrast to the rescue afforded by FGF14bWT, FGF14bR/A did not rescue the key parameters that lead to increased inactivation observed after FGF14 shRNA. NaV late current and the time constant of inactivation were not different from shRNA (Figure 4D–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: FGF14bR/A does not rescue resurgent NaV current after FGF14 shRNA knockdown.
source: Consistent with these findings, we observed the expected reduction in resurgent NaV current (Figure 4G–H).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4G-H.

claim: The FGF14 N-terminus must exert its key effects through FGF14's direct interaction with the NaV C-terminus.
source: Thus, the FGF14 N-terminus must exert its key effects through FGF14's direct interaction with the NaV C-terminus.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that FGF14bR/A, which cannot bind NaV channels, fails to rescue the effects of FGF14 knockdown.

claim: FGF14 knockdown markedly increases the current threshold to produce an action potential in cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: Figure 5A–B and Table 2 show that FGF14 knockdown and expression of the dominant negative FGF14bΔNT markedly increased the current threshold to produce an action potential; other action potential parameters were not affected.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B and Table 2.

claim: Expression of the dominant negative FGF14bΔNT markedly increases the current threshold to produce an action potential in cerebellar Purkinje neurons.
source: Figure 5A–B and Table 2 show that FGF14 knockdown and expression of the dominant negative FGF14bΔNT markedly increased the current threshold to produce an action potential; other action potential parameters were not affected.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B and Table 2.

claim: FGF14 knockdown and expression of FGF14bΔNT do not affect other action potential parameters besides current threshold.
source: Figure 5A–B and Table 2 show that FGF14 knockdown and expression of the dominant negative FGF14bΔNT markedly increased the current threshold to produce an action potential; other action potential parameters were not affected.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B and Table 2.

claim: Co-expression of FGF14bWT restores the current threshold to control levels after FGF14 knockdown.
source: Rescue of FGF14 knockdown by co-expression of FGF14bWT restored the current threshold to control levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B and Table 2.

claim: FGF14bR/A does not restore the current threshold to control levels after FGF14 knockdown.
source: Rescue with the non-interacting FGF14bR/A did not.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A-B and Table 2.

claim: The number of action potentials evoked during 600 ms current injection is significantly larger in control neurons than in neurons transfected with FGF14 shRNA.
source: We also analyzed the number of actions evoked during 600 ms current injection over a wide range of current amplitudes. The number of action potentials evoked was significantly larger in control (scrambled shRNA) neurons than in neurons transfected with FGF14 shRNA.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Co-expression of FGF14bWT restores the number of evoked action potentials to control levels after FGF14 knockdown.
source: Rescue with FGF14bWT, but not FGF14bR/A, restored the number of evoked action potentials to control levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: FGF14bR/A does not restore the number of evoked action potentials to control levels after FGF14 knockdown.
source: Rescue with FGF14bWT, but not FGF14bR/A, restored the number of evoked action potentials to control levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: Expression of the dominant negative FGF14bΔNT reduces the number of evoked action potentials to the level observed after FGF14 knockdown.
source: Expression of the dominant negative FGF14bΔNT reduced the number of evoked action potentials to the level observed after FGF14 knockdown (Figure 5C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C-D.

claim: FGF14b and its N-terminus specifically is a critical regulator of neuronal firing and intrinsic membrane properties.
source: Thus, as observed for the individual NaV channel kinetic parameters, FGF14b, and its N-terminus specifically, is a critical regulator of neuronal firing and intrinsic membrane properties.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental observations on action potential threshold and evoked action potentials.

source: Rapid firing of cerebellar Purkinje neurons is facilitated in part by a voltage-gated Na+ (NaV) 'resurgent' current, which allows renewed Na+ influx during membrane repolarization.

claim: Resurgent current allows renewed Na+ influx during membrane repolarization.

claim: Cerebellar Purkinje neurons display a repetitive firing behavior driven by voltage-gated Na+ channels.

claim: NaV1.6 inactivation is less complete compared to other NaV channels.

claim: Scn8a-encoded NaV1.6 channels have a relatively large 'late' (non-inactivating) component compared to other resident NaV channels in cerebellar Purkinje neurons.

source: Expression of FGF14ΔNT was even more efficient, resulting in a ∼85% reduction, perhaps because overexpression of FGF14ΔNT was more efficient in replacing endogenous FGF14b than shRNA knockdown was in eliminating endogenous FGF14b.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from Figure 3.

claim: Overexpression of FGF14ΔNT may be more efficient in replacing endogenous FGF14b than shRNA knockdown is in eliminating endogenous FGF14b.
source: Expression of FGF14ΔNT was even more efficient, resulting in a ∼85% reduction, perhaps because overexpression of FGF14ΔNT was more efficient in replacing endogenous FGF14b than shRNA knockdown was in eliminating endogenous FGF14b.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning to explain the observed difference in reduction efficiency.

claim: FGF14 may cooperate with NaVβ4 to generate resurgent current.
source: Thus, FGF14 may cooperate with NaVβ4 to generate resurgent current, perhaps by biasing NaV1.6 channels towards inactivation and thereby disadvantaging the blocking particle.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the experimental observations.

claim: FGF14 may bias NaV1.6 channels away from inactivation and thereby advantage the blocking particle.
source: Thus, FGF14 may cooperate with NaVβ4 to generate resurgent current, perhaps by biasing NaV1.6 channels towards inactivation and thereby disadvantaging the blocking particle.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that FGF14 knockdown biases channels toward inactivation, implying that FGF14 presence biases away from inactivation.

claim: The effects on resurgent current attributed to FGF14 may result from FGF14's overall influence on NaV channel kinetics within Purkinje neurons.
source: Thus, the effects on resurgent current that we attribute to FGF14 may result from FGF14's overall influence of NaV channel kinetics within Purkinje neurons.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning acknowledging that effects are on total NaV current from both NaV1.6 and NaV1.1.

claim: Spinocerebellar ataxia patients with FGF14 haploinsufficiency have more variable phenotypes and decreased penetrance compared to patients with the FGF14bF150S mutation.
source: Our results may also provide some insight into the more variable phenotypes and decreased penetrance in spinocerebellar ataxia patients with FGF14 haploinsufficiency (Dalski et al., 2005; Coebergh et al., 2013) vs patients with a FGF14 mutation (FGF14bF150S) found in a large Dutch spinocerebellar ataxia kindred (van Swieten et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous clinical studies.

claim: The FGF14bF150S mutant exerts a dominant negative mechanism in which the axon initial segment is depleted of NaV channels and NaV current density is reduced in hippocampal neurons.
source: Studies in hippocampal neurons suggest that the FGF14bF150S mutant exerts a dominant negative mechanism in which the axon initial segment is depleted of NaV channels and NaV current density is reduced (Laezza et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: A reduction in NaV current density (with the FGF14bF150S mutation) compared to an effect solely on NaV channel kinetics (with FGF14 haploinsufficiency) may explain the higher penetrance and decreased phenotypic variability in patients with the FGF14bF150S mutation.
source: A reduction in NaV current density (with the FGF14bF150S mutation) compared to an effect solely on NaV channel kinetics (with FGF14 haploinsufficiency) may explain the higher penetrance and decreased phenotypic variability in patients with the FGF14bF150S mutation.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning based on the experimental observations and clinical data.

claim: Studying FHFs in their native cellular context is crucial for defining their specific roles.
source: An important aspect of this study examining effects on NaV channel kinetics was that our analyses were performed in Purkinje neurons. Studying FHFs in their native cellular context appears to be crucial for defining their specific roles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of different results in neurons versus heterologous systems.

claim: Expression of NaV1.6 and FGF14bWT in ND7/23 cells almost eliminates NaV current density.
source: For example, expression of NaV1.6 and FGF14bWT in ND7/23 cells almost eliminated NaV current density (Laezza et al., 2009) while overexpression of FGF14bWT in hippocampal neurons increased NaV current density (Laezza et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Overexpression of FGF14bWT in hippocampal neurons increases NaV current density.
source: For example, expression of NaV1.6 and FGF14bWT in ND7/23 cells almost eliminated NaV current density (Laezza et al., 2009) while overexpression of FGF14bWT in hippocampal neurons increased NaV current density (Laezza et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: Expression of FGF14ΔNT in ND7/23 cells increases current density.
source: Similarly, expression of FGF14ΔNT in ND7/23 cells increased current density, while here we observed that FGF14ΔNT expression in cerebellar Purkinje neurons exerted dominant-negative effects upon NaV channel kinetics, but no consequences for NaV current density.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with previous studies in heterologous systems.

claim: Additional regulatory factors present in neurons may be necessary for physiologic regulation of NaV channels by FHFs.
source: While the etiology of the different results in neurons compared to heterologous expression systems is not known, we speculate that additional regulatory factors present in neurons are necessary for physiologic regulation of NaV channels by FHFs.
evidence: The claim is speculative reasoning to explain differences between neurons and heterologous systems.

claim: FGF13 co-expression reduces NaV1.5 current density in HEK293 cells.
source: Indeed, we have observed similarly disparate results for the related FGF13 and the cardiac NaV1.5 channel. In HEK293 cells, FGF13 co-expression reduces NaV1.5 current density (not shown), but we showed that the role FGF13 in cardiomyocytes is to increase NaV current density (Wang et al., 2011; Hennessey et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is based on unpublished observations by the authors.

claim: The role of FGF13 in cardiomyocytes is to increase NaV current density.
source: Indeed, we have observed similarly disparate results for the related FGF13 and the cardiac NaV1.5 channel. In HEK293 cells, FGF13 co-expression reduces NaV1.5 current density (not shown), but we showed that the role FGF13 in cardiomyocytes is to increase NaV current density (Wang et al., 2011; Hennessey et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Some patients with spinocerebellar ataxia, but not controls, harbor synonymous variants in FGF14.
source: Finally, our data also provide information about possible consequences of FGF14 overexpression, hypothesized as pathologic in rare cases. Some patients with spinocerebellar ataxia, but not controls, harbor synonymous variants in FGF14.
evidence: The claim is based on established clinical observations.

claim: Synonymous variants in FGF14 found in some spinocerebellar ataxia patients encode a more frequently used codon than the wild type sequence.
source: These variants encode a more frequently used codon than the wild type sequence, leading to the hypothesis that patients with these variants would overexpress FGF14 as a cause of disease (Dalski et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: It has been hypothesized that patients with synonymous FGF14 variants would overexpress FGF14 as a cause of disease.
source: These variants encode a more frequently used codon than the wild type sequence, leading to the hypothesis that patients with these variants would overexpress FGF14 as a cause of disease (Dalski et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a previous study presenting this hypothesis.

claim: If synonymous FGF14 variants identified in spinocerebellar ataxia patients are truly associated with disease, mechanisms other than FGF14 overexpression are suggested.
source: Thus, if these variants identified in spinocerebellar ataxia patients are truly associated with disease, our data suggest mechanisms other than FGF14 overexpression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation that FGF14bWT overexpression has no effect.

claim: FGF14 is a critical regulator of the ability of cerebellar Purkinje neuron NaV channels to support resurgent NaV current.
source: In summary, these data add to a growing appreciation of physiologic and pathophysiologic roles for FHFs in neurons. In the case of spinocerebellar ataxia, our data suggest that FGF14 is a critical regulator of the ability of cerebellar Purkinje neuron NaV channels to support resurgent NaV current and thereby allow Purkinje neurons to fire repetitively.
evidence: The claim is supported by the combined experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: FGF14 allows Purkinje neurons to fire repetitively.
source: In summary, these data add to a growing appreciation of physiologic and pathophysiologic roles for FHFs in neurons. In the case of spinocerebellar ataxia, our data suggest that FGF14 is a critical regulator of the ability of cerebellar Purkinje neuron NaV channels to support resurgent NaV current and thereby allow Purkinje neurons to fire repetitively.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The study provides a molecular understanding for the observation that FGF14 regulates Purkinje neuron intrinsic excitability.
source: Thus, we provide a molecular understanding for the observation that FGF14 regulates Purkinje neuron intrinsic excitability (Shakkottai et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined experimental observations and cites a previous study.

claim: FGF14 regulates presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels at the cerebellar granule cell to Purkinje cell synapse.
source: In combination with our data showing that FGF14 also regulates presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels at the cerebellar granule cell to Purkinje cell synapse, these data pinpoint several specific mechanisms by which mutations in FGF14 underlie spinocerebellar ataxia.
evidence: The claim is based on previous work by the authors.

claim: The data pinpoint several specific mechanisms by which mutations in FGF14 underlie spinocerebellar ataxia.

claim: 8–10% of cerebellar Purkinje neurons cultured for ≤14 days in vitro exhibit spontaneous action potentials.
source: Under our culture conditions (≤14 days in vitro), we found that 8–10% of cerebellar Purkinje neurons exhibit spontaneous action potentials (firing rate 5–20 Hz) with regular and irregular patterns.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: Spontaneous action potentials in cultured Purkinje neurons (≤14 days in vitro) have a firing rate of 5–20 Hz with regular and irregular patterns.
source: Under our culture conditions (≤14 days in vitro), we found that 8–10% of cerebellar Purkinje neurons exhibit spontaneous action potentials (firing rate 5–20 Hz) with regular and irregular patterns.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations.

claim: ∼50% of Purkinje neurons cultured for >20 days in vitro spontaneously fire.
source: When neurons were cultured for extended periods (>20 days in vitro), we observed that ∼50% of Purkinje neurons spontaneously fired—more similar to acutely isolated Purkinje neurons (Raman and Bean, 1999) and cultured Purkinje neurons (Gruol and Franklin, 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations and citations to previous studies.

claim: Spontaneous activity in cultured Purkinje neurons depends upon the maturity of the neurons in culture.
source: These data suggest that spontaneous activity depends upon the maturity of the neurons in culture.
